作為印度古典舞者腳上小金屬鈴串，腳鈴在傳統演出中綁於腳踝上方，用以強化節奏並讓複: As strings of small metal bells worn by classical Indian dancers, ghungroo are tied above the ankle in traditional performance to reinforce the rhythm and make complex footwork audible; a child beginner may start with about fifty bells and increase to more than two hundred with age and skill. The name differs slightly between the languages of India, and folk dancers in Nepal use a similar bell strap, nine to twenty-seven small bronze bells sewn onto a cloth band and tied at the ankle, the number chosen to suit the words of the song. V. Anuradha Singh developed a style of music built on the bells, performed at festivals of pure music where dance is not allowed, using the footwork as percussion art for up to a hundred minutes without a break and without moving from the spot.
將腳鈴（Ghungroo）綁於腳踝上方，使鈴串貼合外踝與內踝；發聲靠踏步、點地與: The ghungroo are tied above the ankle so that the strings of bells sit against the outer and inner ankle; the sound comes from stepping, tapping the ground and continuous footwork, which makes the small metal bells strike each other and produce the rhythm. A beginner can start with about fifty bells and add more with age and skill; in practice, first mark the beat with a steady step pattern and then gradually add more complex combinations. In performance the number and size of the bells can be chosen as needed, and the force of the step controlled so that the rhythm is clearly heard.

Indian ghungroo are usually several bells strung into a ring and fixed with knotted cord. The Nepalese form uses nine to twenty-seven small bronze bells sewn onto a cloth band about twenty-three centimetres long and seven and a half wide, which is then tied at the ankle. Beyond the bells, the cloth band and the cord, the source does not state the materials of other parts.
脚铃的声音来自多枚小型金属铃相互碰撞，音高会随金属成分与铃的大小显著变化，因此没: The sound of the ghungroo comes from several small metal bells striking one another, and the pitch varies markedly with the alloy and the size of the bells, so there is no fixed range. Volume and rhythmic density depend on the footwork and the number of bells; a string may consist of fifty to more than two hundred bells, while the Nepalese form uses nine to twenty-seven small bronze bells sewn onto cloth. It is not a single bell but many small bells strung together and tied above the ankle, set off by the steps of the dance, to reinforce the rhythm and let the audience hear complex footwork.

腳鈴主要出現在古典印度舞的傳統表演中，如婆羅多（Bharatnatyam）、卡塔: The ghungroo appear mainly in traditional performances of classical Indian dance such as Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kuchipudi, Mohiniyattam, Lavani and Odissi, to reinforce the rhythm and let the audience hear complex footwork. Folk dancers in Nepal also tie talbaja or chap at the ankle, choosing a version with more or fewer bells to suit the words of the song. There is also the form known as ghunghroo vadan, developed by V. Anuradha Singh, in which continuous foot percussion becomes the main music at festivals of pure music where dance is not allowed.
腳鈴（Ghungroo）是將多個小型金屬鈴串連成環、綁在舞者腳踝上方的體鳴樂器，: The ghungroo are an idiophone made of several small metal bells strung into a ring and tied above a dancer's ankle; they are a small idiophone, sounded by shaking or striking. The dancer's complex footwork makes the strings of bells collide, reinforcing the rhythm of the dance and letting the audience hear the steps. They are used mainly in traditional performances of classical Indian dance such as Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kuchipudi, Mohiniyattam, Lavani and Odissi; folk dancers in Nepal also use a similar ring of bells tied at the ankle.
